Name: The Judicial Power of the Carthaginian Court of the Hundred and Four and the Constitutional Powers of the Suffetes
RagShortTexts: The highest civil magistrates of Carthage were the two suffetes elected each year
The Court of the Hundred and Four, made up of one hundred and four aristocratic judges for life, monopolized judicial trials
The appointment and dismissal of overseas commanders and their accountability for defeats were all controlled by the court, leaving no strategic independence
BaseText: Classical scholars regarded the constitution of the city of Carthage as a mixed constitution of commercial aristocratic oligarchy. The highest everyday executive and civil heads were the two 'suffetes' (Suffetes, meaning judges) elected each year by the assembly of aristocratic citizens; their functions were similar to those of Roman consuls, but they had no right to lead troops in war directly. The body that actually monopolized the city's supreme judicial power over life and death was the 'Court of the Hundred and Four' (Court of the Hundred and Four), selected from among the elders. It was originally set up to prevent generals at the head of armies from seizing power in a military coup, and every commander returning home from the front had to submit to the court's extremely harsh audit of his campaign accounts and to military trial. In the Punic Wars, however, the court was controlled by the conservative merchant faction, and its harsh scrutiny of overseas generals, who were constantly threatened with crucifixion, greatly stifled the independence of commanders at the front.

Variants.Content: The one hundred and four venerable judges are the Republic's wall of bronze and iron against the ambitions of tyrants! If generals commanding great armies were not closely supervised, Carthage would long ago have become the warlord fief of Mago or Hannibal!

Those old fools sitting in the hall of Salammbo have turned the law code into a noose for persecuting loyal men! The soldiers at the front trade their blood for land, while they are pondering which hero to nail to a stake after a defeat!

The suffetes of Carthage are mere puppets, and the Court of the Hundred and Four cares only for its ledgers of silver coins. How can a city ruled by peddlers and pettifoggers stand against the iron-hard Roman legions?

Keywords: Court of the Hundred and Four
